profile.address: 215 East Indian School Road, Phoenix, AZ 85012
profile.reading:
This is a small, old, urban telephone building that now sells colocation, and the county record makes that plain. Maricopa County assessor parcel 118-25-125 contains this record's coordinates and carries the situs address 215 East Indian School Road, Phoenix, Arizona 85012. The county places it in legal class 1.11, telecommunications, under property use code 5600, telecommunications property. The lot is 54,530 square feet, about 1.25 acres. That is a central office footprint on a central Phoenix corner, not a wholesale campus on the edge of the valley. The registered owner is recorded as Qwest, with a mailing address at 6300 South Syracuse Way, Englewood, Colorado, the tax office that has followed the old US West and Qwest local exchange estate through every corporate name since. The deed on file was recorded in 2001. The county's ZIP for the parcel is 85012, not the 85013 this registry previously carried.

Lumen Technologies is what that estate is called now. CenturyLink acquired Qwest in 2011, acquired Level 3 Communications on 1 November 2017, renamed itself Lumen on 14 September 2020 and changed its ticker from CTL to LUMN four days later. Lumen sells this kind of building as network colocation rather than as wholesale data centre space. Its own colocation data sheet claims more than 175 carrier neutral data centres across more than 60 North American markets and quotes cabinet power in a 3 to 15 kilowatt range that it says varies by site. Lumen publishes no square footage, no megawatt figure and no address for any individual site, and this one is no exception.

The county roll shows something worth pointing at. The parcel carries a land full cash value of $3,271,800 and no improvement value at all. The building is standing and in service, but its value is not on the local roll, which is consistent with Arizona treating telecommunications company property separately from ordinary locally assessed commercial property. The Arizona Department of Revenue publishes a dedicated telecommunications company property tax form, Form 82056, filed under A.R.S. sections 42-14001 to 42-14005 and 42-14401 to 42-14404. The practical consequence for this registry is that the county cannot supply the building square footage or improvement value it supplies for a conventional data centre parcel.

Phoenix adopted its first zoning definition of a data centre only on 2 July 2025, decades after this exchange was placed in service, and the debate that produced it is not about buildings like this one. Arizona Public Service reports an uncommitted queue of 19.0 gigawatts of large load requests against data centres making up about 5 percent of its 2025 peak. At the Arizona Corporation Commission's large load workshop on 16 April 2026, staff counted about two dozen operating data centres in Arizona with more than 2,000 MW of operating capacity and more than 10,600 MW planned. A 1.25 acre telephone building with a few hundred cabinets sits at the opposite end of that distribution and is easy to mistake for the thing being argued about.

What is not known: no IT load, utility service capacity or standby generation figure is published for this site, the electric utility serving the parcel was not confirmed from a primary source, and the building's floor area does not appear in the county record.

profile.capacity_note: Nothing is published for this site under any of the four power headings. Lumen gives no IT load, no utility service capacity and no standby generation figure for any of its colocation buildings. The only power figure Lumen publishes company wide is a cabinet power range of 3 to 15 kilowatts that it says varies by site, which is a range across 175 or more buildings rather than a figure for this one, so it is not recorded as a value here.
profile.research_note: Updated 2026-09-05. Maricopa County GIS parcel query at the stored coordinates returns parcel 118-25-125, situs 215 East Indian School Road, Phoenix 85012, owner recorded as Qwest with the Englewood, Colorado mailing address, legal class 1.11 telecommunications, land value only with no improvement value on the roll, 1.25 acres. Parcel centroid is about 60 feet from the stored point, so the address is safe to store. The prior source for Arizona power context was a solar installer blog and has been replaced with the Arizona Corporation Commission workshop summary and APS own disclosure.
profile.community_note: The Arizona Corporation Commission held a large load and data centre workshop on 16 April 2026 covering existing Arizona regulatory tools, other states approaches, consumer protections and utility positions. Figures put on the record there included about two dozen operating data centres in Arizona with more than 2,000 MW of operating capacity and more than 10,600 MW of additional capacity planned, Salt River Project serving 59 large load customers with a combined load of nearly 7,000 MW, and Arizona Public Service estimating large customer peak demand of about 13.1 gigawatts. Separately, APS states on its own site that it holds an uncommitted queue of 19.0 gigawatts, forecasts a 12.0 gigawatt data centre peak in 2035, and that data centres made up about 5 percent of its 2025 peak. APS proposed a 45 percent rate increase for extra large energy users in its June 2025 rate request and has served that class under extra high load factor rates descended from a high load factor rate it built in 2017.
profile.regulatory_note: Siting jurisdiction is the City of Phoenix. The parcel is recorded by Maricopa County in legal class 1.11, telecommunications, under property use code 5600, and lies in taxing district 081300, Osborn School District in the City of Phoenix. Phoenix had no zoning definition of a data centre until text amendment Z-TA-2-25-Y, adopted by the Mayor and Council on 2 July 2025, which permits data centres only in the C-2, C-3, CP/GCP, A-1 and A-2 districts with a Special Permit and adds a 150 foot mechanical equipment setback, a 2,640 foot separation from approved high capacity transit stations, an ambient plus 5 percent noise cap near residential zoning, and a two year utility will serve letter requirement. This building long predates that ordinance and the city record does not show a data centre special permit for the parcel.

reading.body:
This is a 1.25-acre urban telephone exchange in central Phoenix, not a wholesale data center campus. Lumen publishes no IT load, utility service capacity, or standby generation for this site, and the county assessor records only land value with no improvement value, consistent with Arizona's separate taxation of telecommunications property. The building predates Phoenix's 2025 data center zoning ordinance and carries no special permit under that code. Its role in the grid is unknown and cannot be assessed from published data.

Arizona Public Service faces an uncommitted queue of 19.0 gigawatts of large load requests, forecasts data center peak demand of 12.0 gigawatts by 2035, and serves 59 large load customers with a combined 7,000 megawatts. At the Arizona Corporation Commission's April 2026 workshop, staff counted about two dozen operating data centers in Arizona with over 2,000 megawatts of capacity and over 10,600 megawatts planned. This one Lumen building, with a few hundred cabinets on a corner lot, sits at the opposite end of that distribution and does not materially constrain or relieve that queue.

Among 57 mapped facilities in Arizona, only four publish power figures totaling 512 megawatts. This site ranks fifth by published capacity in the state, a ranking that reflects the absence of published figures at the other 53 sites rather than the significance of this one. For a reader assessing whether this campus matters to AI scaling, the answer turns on whether Lumen will publish its load: without it, this building is indistinguishable from any other carrier hotel and contributes nothing to the visible grid constraint on compute.
